source.title: How Do Language Models Represent and Use Phonological Information for Allomorph Selection?

record.tranche_reason: Uses FutureLens top-k agreement to test future-token forecasting in new settings, and adds causal steering of the forecasted phonological feature.
record.gate_note: The paper tests forecasting from the position where an allomorph is predicted to the following trigger token, and intervenes on the mapped feature. Embedding-direction classification and nonce-token allomorph results are not rows for these claim versions: they do not measure future-token forecasting. Random-token FutureLens conditions are recorded as controls. Figure-only results are not estimated from plots.
record.test_reason: Applies the original Future Lens probe (top-k agreement for the token at t+2) to allomorph-prediction positions. It compares against matched random-token controls, then steers a forecast-derived phonological direction and measures article/allomorph flips. Its own results bear on V2 (future-token decodability) and V5 (look-ahead in a non-verse task), and partly on V6.
record.recipe_differences: Uses FutureLens top-k forecasting in new allomorph-selection settings, with an orthogonality constraint and an inverse-map steering intervention. This is not a rhyme-planning replication.
record.method_sensitivity: Forecasting and steering vary by model, language, and layer; steering strengthens in later layers. The main English and cross-lingual analyses use top-1 consistency-filtered examples; the random-token control has lower forecasting agreement.

fits_no_version.finding: The phonological vowel/consonant feature lies on one linear direction in trigger-token embeddings. Varying it in nonce tokens shifts a/an and cross-linguistic allomorph choice (token-level wug tests).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Models encode phonological conditioning of allomorphy as a single embedding direction that causally drives allomorph choice.

fits_no_version.finding: The same direction does not reliably shift explicit yes/no sound judgments about nonce tokens (Figure 6).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Phonological features used in generation are dissociated from metalinguistic sound judgments.

record.peer_reviewed: Proceedings of the 2026 Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing
record.problems: The authors note that phonological labels are derived from corpus patterns rather than observed pronunciations and may be noisy. The forecasting mechanism is inferred through an auxiliary FutureLens probe, and the study does not identify the exact computations. Forecasts are tested at t+2, not at longer distances. Relevant forecast and steering results generally have no uncertainty estimates stated.
record.rows_left_out: No relevant rows left out. Embedding-direction classification, nonce allomorph-choice sweeps, and explicit sound-judgment results do not measure the claim versions’ future-token forecasting or rhyme-planning constructs.

untested.parts: No frontier model, no rhyming verse, no rhyme-candidate intervention.
Only the t+2 horizon (one token beyond the next) is tested; no longer distances. Results come from top-1 consistency-filtered examples only.
The forecast is used for the current next token (the article), not cached for later positions; pre-caching versus myopic computation is not tested.
No rhyme planning in open models; no attribution graphs.
No multi-step reasoning, chess or Sokoban; only decoder-only transformers.
Longer-horizon planning is not tested, so the 'only a few tokens ahead' part is neither supported nor challenged. Local heuristics are not explicitly ruled out (no control steering direction).

missing.what: Layer dissociation: the forecast is accurate mid-network, but the steering effect appears only in the final few layers. This bears on whether the forecast is what drives the choice.
missing.locator: Appendix D results; Appendix F results; Figures 4, 10, 11

missing.what: Article-probability shifts under steering (P(an) up, P(a) down, and the reverse), figure only.
Ordinary vs orthogonal FutureLens comparison showing that peak late-layer top-5 agreement is preserved (methodological robustness for the forecast rows).

record.verdict_notes: The steering direction is W^T d, applied at the position that predicts the article itself. With no random-direction or a/an-logit-direction control, a large flip rate does not on its own show that a planned feature, rather than the local readout, is being manipulated. This is why V6 is labelled limits_scope rather than challenges. The random-token controls are themselves fairly high (37–57%), and all forecast results use top-1 consistency-filtered examples. No uncertainty estimates are given for the forecast or steering numbers.

versions.untested_parts: No rhyming verse, candidate rhyme words, or intervention on rhyme candidates.
Forecasting is tested for the trigger at t+2, with one intervening allomorph token; longer look-ahead distances are not tested.
The study does not test whether a feature is computed at one position because it will help later positions rather than as a side effect of next-token prediction.
No rhyme-planning test in open-weight models using open attribution-graph or probing tools.
Tests phonologically conditioned allomorph selection, not multi-step reasoning, chess, or Sokoban; it does not compare architectures beyond the models reported.
The study tests causal use at a short t+2 horizon, but does not compare longer horizons or test whether the same effect is explained by local next-token heuristics.

relationships.condition: Allomorph-prediction positions in English (1B–70B instruct models), French and Italian; trigger at t+2; late layers; filtered examples
relationships.reason: Top-5 trigger agreement far exceeds random-token controls: about 90% peak in small models; 81.8% vs 45.1% (70B); 94.8% vs 57.0% (French); 91.4% vs 36.9% (Italian) (R1–R3, R10, R15, R17).
relationships.display_finding: Top-5 trigger agreement peaked around 90% in small models and reached 81.8% versus 45.1% for 70B, 94.8% versus 57.0% for French, and 91.4% versus 36.9% for Italian.

source_check.reason: The support label is warranted, but the condition needs correction: French uses special alignment because l’ spans two tokens; a common t+2 offset from allomorph prediction is not established. R1–R3, R10, R15 and R17 otherwise support decodability.

relationships.condition: Phonologically conditioned allomorph selection (a/an, le/la vs l', un/uno) in Llama, Qwen, Gemma, Lucie and Minerva instruct models
relationships.reason: The upcoming trigger is decodable at the allomorph position, and steering its forecast-mapped phonological direction flips the current choice: 84–90% in English small models, 86.1% in 70B, 74.9% French, 66.3% Italian (R1–R3, R7–R10, R12–R15, R17, R19–R24).
relationships.display_finding: Upcoming phonological triggers were decodable before generation, and steering flipped current choices in 84–90% of English small-model cases, 86.1% for the 70B model, 74.9% in French, and 66.3% in Italian.
